candidates.label: Mount of Olives
candidates.support: Wikidata's coordinate for the ridge is corroborated by OpenBible.info's independently recorded point for the same feature.

summary.text: The Mount of Olives is the ridge east of Jerusalem's Old City, separated from the city and the Temple Mount by the Kidron Valley; the Jewish historian Josephus places it about six furlongs (just over 1 km) from the city. Its name comes from the olive trees that have grown on its slopes for thousands of years. Its eastern side descends past the villages of Bethphage and Bethany toward the Judean Desert and the Dead Sea. Its slopes had long been used for burials: after David took the city, a number of Israelites chose to be buried there.

history.text: The Gospels describe Jesus coming up from Jericho to Bethphage and Bethany at the Mount of Olives and sending two disciples ahead from there before his entry into Jerusalem; Luke says the crowd of disciples began to praise God "at the descent of the Mount of Olives." Matthew says he was sitting on the mount when his disciples asked him privately about "the end of the age." Luke says that in his last days he taught in the Temple by day and spent each night on the mount, and Matthew, Mark and Luke all say he went out to the mount on the night of his arrest. Acts records the disciples returning to Jerusalem from "the mountain called Olivet," a Sabbath day's journey away.

The Old Testament already names the ridge: 2 Samuel describes King David going up it weeping as he fled from his son Absalom, and Zechariah pictures a day when "his feet will stand... on the Mount of Olives." Such prophecies linked the mount with a day of judgment and the resurrection of the righteous, which helps explain why it became a favored burial place. During the siege of AD 70, Josephus says, a Roman legion camped on the mount.

Today the ridge carries several churches marking events in the Gospels and Acts, among them the Franciscan sanctuaries of Bethphage and Dominus Flevit ("the Lord wept"), the Church of the Pater Noster and the Chapel of the Ascension, alongside the large Jewish cemetery that covers much of its slopes. The summit gives one of the best-known views of Jerusalem, and to the north, Mount Scopus is the site of the Hebrew University.

scripture.textWEB: They came to Jericho. As he went out from Jericho with his disciples and a great multitude, the son of Timaeus, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, was sitting by the road.
When they came near to Jerusalem and came to Bethsphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples,
As he sat on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately, saying, “Tell us, when will these things be? What is the sign of your coming, and of the end of the age?”
When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
When they came near to Jerusalem, to Bethsphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples
As he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter, James, John, and Andrew asked him privately,
When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
When he came near to Bethsphage and Bethany, at the mountain that is called Olivet, he sent two of his disciples,
As he was now getting near, at the descent of the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works which they had seen,
Every day Jesus was teaching in the temple, and every night he would go out and spend the night on the mountain that is called Olivet.
He came out and went, as his custom was, to the Mount of Olives. His disciples also followed him.
but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives.
Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mountain called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away.

otConnections.note: Zechariah's prophecy that 'his feet will stand in that day on the Mount of Olives' (a coming day of the Lord) is widely noted as background for the mount's later Jewish and Christian eschatological associations.
David's flight over the Mount of Olives during Absalom's revolt is the earliest narrative use of the mountain as a named place on a route out of Jerusalem.

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod the Great (ruler: Herod the Great)
Ethnarchy of Judea, Samaria and Idumea (ruler: Herod Archelaus)
politicalHistory.note: The emperor Augustus did not grant Archelaus the royal title his father's will asked for, only "ethnarch." This area's drawn shape also includes Gaza and the coastal strip north to Rhinocolura; Josephus records that Augustus took Gaza itself, with Gadara and Hippos, from Herod's kingdom at his death and added it to the province of Syria, but since none of these is its own area on this map, Gaza's land and this coastal strip stay within the area around them.

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Judea (ruler: Prefects, e.g. Pontius Pilate)
politicalHistory.note: Luke links a census "when Quirinius was governor of Syria" to Jesus' birth, which Luke and Matthew place in Herod's days; the Jewish historian Josephus dates Quirinius's own census of Judea to this year. This map takes no position on how the accounts relate. This area's drawn shape also includes Gaza and the coastal strip north to Rhinocolura, which stayed in the province of Syria from 4 BC on (rule 4, as in the previous period's note).
